questions.prompt: A triangular display has 11 rows. Each row has 2 more tiles than the row above, and the display uses 275 tiles. How many tiles are in the bottom row?
questions.hint: Which row has as many tiles as the average row?

lessons.headline: Make the shared part cancel
lessons.intro: If two bundles have an identical part, compare what is left after removing that part from each. When the parts do not yet match, you can make several copies of a whole bundle. Its total must grow by the same factor.

example.prompt: A tin and a ball weigh 180 g together. The same tin and three identical balls weigh 260 g. How heavy is a ball?
steps: The same tin appears on both scales, so the extra 80 g comes from the two extra balls.
One ball weighs 80 ÷ 2 = 40 g. The tin weighs 140 g, which fits both weighings.

lessons.bridge: In the film, follow the marker through the two stationery orders. Watch which entire order gets doubled before the subtraction works.
lessons.recap: Choose one kind of object to cancel. Match its count by scaling whole bundles, subtract in the same order on both sides, then put your answer back into an original bundle.

questions.title: Spools
questions.prompt: A box with 4 identical spools weighs 710 g. The same box with 7 of those spools weighs 995 g. What is the mass of one spool in grams?
questions.hint: Which items appear on only one side after matching the boxes?

questions.title: The printed cards
questions.prompt: Printing 3 large cards and 2 small cards costs 29 dollars. Printing 4 large and 4 small costs 44 dollars. What does one large card cost in dollars?
questions.hint: Make two copies of the first order. Which size then has the same count?

questions.title: Music loops
questions.prompt: Two drum loops and three bell loops, played end to end, last 38 seconds. Three drum loops and two bell loops last 37 seconds. Each loop of a given kind has the same length. How many seconds is one bell loop?
questions.hint: Compare the two recordings. Which single loop has replaced another?

questions.title: Two bands of seats
questions.prompt: A hall repeats two row sizes, wide and narrow. Four wide rows and three narrow rows seat 138 people. Six wide rows and five narrow rows seat 216. How many people fit in five wide rows and four narrow rows?
questions.hint: Could you make twice the seating arrangement you want by combining the two given arrangements?

lessons.headline: One day’s amount or the running total?
lessons.intro: Doubling gives a tidy connection between a single amount and all the earlier amounts. A running total includes everything from the first day up to the day named. A day’s own amount includes just that day.

example.prompt: A game awards 5 shells, then 10, then 20. How many shells have you collected after the third award?
steps: The third award alone is 20 shells. The three awards together give 5 + 10 + 20 = 35.
The next award would be 40. The total of 35 is exactly one starting award below that.

lessons.bridge: As the film doubles a whole row of terms, look for what cancels. That cancellation explains how one more day can put a project over budget.
lessons.recap: Mark the first term. To find one term, count doublings. To add consecutive doubling terms, subtract the first amount from the next term after the sum. A budget check needs the totals on both sides of the limit.
lessons.videoTitle: Doubling, geometric growth and finite sums

questions.title: Before the copier ran
questions.prompt: A copier doubles the number of copies on each run. After three runs there are 72 copies. How many were there before the first run?
questions.hint: Trace the three runs in reverse.

questions.title: Four envelopes
questions.prompt: Four envelopes hold, in order, 6, 12, 24 and 48 tickets. A fifth would contain 96. How many tickets are in the first four together?
questions.hint: Double the sum of the first four envelopes and compare the two sums.

questions.title: The seed grant
questions.prompt: A fund pays 9 dollars on its first day and doubles the payment every day. It has 560 dollars available. How many more dollars does it need to make all six daily payments?
questions.hint: Find the total cost through day six before comparing it with the grant.

questions.title: Folded paper
questions.prompt: A strip of paper is folded in half five times. It starts as one layer. Each fold adds one new crease through every current layer, at a fresh position on the strip. Once unfolded, how many crease positions are there?
questions.hint: Count how many layers receive a new crease at each fold.

lessons.headline: Count the ways into each position
lessons.intro: When many paths branch and meet again, it helps to count their endings. If you know how a path can arrive at one position, you can use counts from earlier positions to build the next count.

example.prompt: A frog starts at stone 0 and jumps forward by one or two stones at a time. How many different ways can it reach stone 3?
steps: There is one way to reach stone 1. Stone 2 has two routes, a jump of 2 or two jumps of 1.
To reach 3, add a jump of 1 to either route to 2, or a jump of 2 to the route to 1. There are 2 + 1 = 3 ways.

lessons.bridge: In the film, first watch the number that stays fixed as a reading changes. On the ladder, watch which route counts survive when a rung is broken.
lessons.recap: A repeated rule needs a starting value. For routes, give the start one empty route and count distinct kinds of last move. A forbidden landing has zero routes, even if a longer jump can pass over it.

questions.title: Three button presses
questions.prompt: A machine displays 3. Each time you press its button, it doubles the displayed number and then adds 1. What number does it display after three presses?
questions.hint: The starting value is the reading before any press.

questions.title: Message chain
questions.prompt: A number starts at 5. Each turn doubles the number and subtracts 3. What number appears after six turns?
questions.hint: Track how far the number is above 3.

questions.title: The cracked tile
questions.prompt: A robot moves from tile 0 to tile 7 by jumps of 1 or 2. Tile 4 cannot be landed on. How many different jump sequences reach tile 7 exactly?
questions.hint: Fill in a route count for every tile. Put a zero at tile 4.

questions.title: Signal words
questions.prompt: A transmitter fills exactly 8 time slots with short pulses lasting 1 slot and long pulses lasting 3 slots. Pulses follow one another with no gap. How many different pulse sequences can it send?
questions.hint: If the last pulse is long, how many slots did the earlier pulses fill?

lessons.headline: Which rectangle wins?
lessons.intro: Two rectangles can use the same length of edging and enclose different areas. First count the lengths that actually use the edging. Then ask how far you can move the dimensions towards balance while still satisfying the rules.

example.prompt: An 18 cm loop of string makes a rectangle with whole-centimetre sides. Compare the 2 cm by 7 cm rectangle with the 4 cm by 5 cm rectangle.
steps: In each case the adjacent sides add to 9 cm, so the whole perimeter is 18 cm.
The areas are 14 cm² and 20 cm². With the same side sum, bringing the two side lengths closer has gained area.

figure.alt: A two-by-seven rectangle and a four-by-five rectangle drawn on the same centimetre scale.

lessons.bridge: Watch what changes in the film when one side of the pen sits against a wall. Decide which two quantities now need to balance.
lessons.recap: Draw and count the charged or fenced edges first. For a fixed sum the closest eligible pair has the largest product. Whole-number restrictions can rule out a perfect balance or create a tie.
lessons.videoTitle: Optimising areas and lengths under constraints

questions.title: The garden frame
questions.prompt: A rectangle has whole-centimetre sides and a 30 cm perimeter. What is its greatest possible area in square centimetres?
questions.hint: The two adjacent side lengths share half the perimeter.

questions.title: Shelf dividers
questions.prompt: A rectangular display is exactly 18 cm long along one edge. Its perimeter may be at most 50 cm. What is its largest possible area in square centimetres?
questions.hint: Take both 18 cm edges out of the allowance first.

questions.title: The narrow garden
questions.prompt: A garden borders a shed wall. A 32 m fence covers the other three sides exactly. Each of the two equal sides that run out from the wall must be at most 5 m long, in whole metres. What is the greatest possible area in square metres?
questions.hint: Use 32 minus two widths for the third side. Check all five allowed widths.

questions.title: Two pens
questions.prompt: Two identical rectangular pens share one divider. They sit side by side to make one rectangle. The divider joins the front fence to the back fence. All fences together measure 42 m, and each pen has whole-metre sides. What is the greatest combined area in square metres?
questions.hint: Let each pen be w metres wide and d deep. Count two stretches of width 2w and three stretches of depth d.

lessons.headline: Find where the loop begins
lessons.intro: Imagine pausing a machine and writing down everything you need to predict its next move. That record is its state. With a fixed rule, seeing the same full state twice tells you exactly which moves will repeat.

example.prompt: A lamp starts white. Each press changes it to the next colour in this rule: white → red → blue → green → red. What colour is it after four presses?
steps: The first press makes red. Presses two and three make blue and green.
The fourth press brings back red. White was a starting colour outside the three-colour loop.

lessons.bridge: Track the pair of dials in the film. In the numbered machine, listen for the move that takes you into the loop before you start counting full laps.
lessons.recap: Write the whole state at move zero, then stop when a full state repeats. Subtract any lead-in moves first. An exact number of laps brings you back to the loop entry.

questions.title: Turn the arrow
questions.prompt: A pointer starts facing east. Each move turns it through a quarter turn anticlockwise. Which direction does it face after 26 moves? Enter north, east, south or west.
questions.hint: Four anticlockwise quarter turns restore the pointer.

questions.title: Two wheels
questions.prompt: A lock has a 4-position wheel and a 6-position wheel. A click advances both by one position. After how many positive clicks do both first return to their starting positions?
questions.hint: Write the first few reset counts for each wheel.

questions.title: Museum lights
questions.prompt: A light starts amber. After one tick it is white, then it cycles through red, green, blue and red again. What colour is the light after 100 ticks? Enter one colour.
questions.hint: At which tick does red first appear?

questions.title: A walker on a strip
questions.prompt: Five squares are labelled 0 to 4 in a row. A counter starts on 1 moving right. Each move advances it one square. On arriving at an end it reverses direction for its next move. Which square does it occupy after 83 moves?
questions.hint: List the square and the direction together. Square 1 can be visited facing either way.

lessons.headline: Which digits are free to choose?
lessons.intro: In a palindrome, choosing a digit also chooses its mirror partner. This changes both a counting problem and a divisibility test. A centre digit in an odd-length number contributes just once.

example.prompt: How many three-digit palindromes begin with 4 and have an even middle digit?
steps: The last digit must be 4, leaving just the middle place to choose.
The choices 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8 give five numbers, from 404 to 484.

lessons.bridge: When the film splits 3663 into two pairs of digits, notice the value of each pair. Later, ask when two different centre digits can both pass the divisibility test.
lessons.recap: Write the free positions and mirror them before testing any condition. A first digit must be nonzero, but a centre may be zero. When a digit sum must be a multiple of 9, check whether both 0 and 9 fit.

questions.title: Mirror total
questions.prompt: A five-digit palindrome begins with 28 and its middle digit is 3. What is the sum of its digits?
questions.hint: Write all five places before adding.

questions.title: One free digit
questions.prompt: How many three-digit palindromes beginning with 9 are divisible by 9?
questions.hint: Try both ends of the digit range for the middle digit.

questions.title: Four places
questions.prompt: How many four-digit palindromes are divisible by 3 and end in 2?
questions.hint: If the last digit is 2, the first digit is already fixed.

questions.title: The vanishing digit
questions.prompt: A six-digit palindrome uses only digits 1 to 9. Erasing its first and last digits leaves a four-digit palindrome. The sum of all six digits is 26, and the four remaining digits sum to 18. How many original numbers are possible?
questions.hint: Use the lost digit sum to recover the outer pair. Then pair the free inner digits.

lessons.headline: Build a list you know is complete
lessons.intro: When several conditions interact, give the list a definite order. Fix one choice, work out all its legal endings, and only then move on. Often you only need to write a few row totals.

example.prompt: Which pairs of different positive whole numbers add to 9, with the smaller number written first?
steps: Try the smaller number in order. The first four pairs are (1, 8), (2, 7), (3, 6) and (4, 5).
Starting at 5 would put the larger number first. Every allowed pair has appeared once.

lessons.bridge: Watch how the film labels its boxes. Swapping two values can create a new answer when the labels stay fixed. Then look for the first and last legal entry in each row.
lessons.recap: Pick a short list of first choices and keep the labels straight. Use each condition to find a row’s two endpoints. Count both endpoints and stop where the remaining choices become impossible.

questions.title: Small change
questions.prompt: Nina pays exactly 18 cents using only 2-cent and 5-cent coins. How many different combinations of coin counts are possible? The order of the coins does not matter.
questions.hint: Fix the number of 5-cent coins. What must be true of the amount left?

questions.title: Two switches
questions.prompt: Two labelled switches A and B each display an integer from 0 to 5. Their readings add to 6. How many different displays are possible?
questions.hint: Fix A. Which value of B is then forced?

questions.title: Archery scores
questions.prompt: An archery target has four scoring rings worth 2, 3, 5 or 8 points. A player hits one ring with each of three arrows and scores 13 in total. How many different lists of the three scores in shooting order are possible?
questions.hint: Split by whether an arrow scored 8. Within each group, find the possible three scores before ordering them.

questions.title: Moving on the grid
questions.prompt: A token starts at (0, 0) and chooses a destination (x, y). Both coordinates are whole numbers from 0 to 6. The token must move at least 4 but no more than 6 steps, moving only right or up. How many different destinations are possible?
questions.hint: Group destinations by x + y, the number of steps. Multiple routes to one point count once.

lessons.headline: What makes two choices different?
lessons.intro: Before multiplying, describe what the finished choice looks like. A badge with a symbol and a colour has different places to fill. A group of people doing the same job stays the same group however you list their names.

example.prompt: A reading club has four books. You may borrow two different books as a pair. How many pairs are there?
steps: There are 4 choices for the first book and 3 for the next, giving 12 ordered lists.
Every pair appears in two lists, one in each order. Halving 12 gives 6 pairs.

lessons.bridge: In the film, compare choosing a flavour and a topping with choosing two helpers. Keep that distinction in mind when the four-person team has several possible mixtures of skills.
lessons.recap: Multiply choices that together make one outcome. When several people or objects have identical roles, remove the extra orders of selection. Add alternative group patterns only after checking they are disjoint.

questions.title: Signal flags
questions.prompt: A flag has one of 4 background colours, one of 3 border styles and one of 2 centre symbols. Every combination is allowed. How many flags are possible?
questions.hint: Fix a background and count its border-and-symbol choices.

questions.title: Two librarians
questions.prompt: Six students volunteer. Two different volunteers will work together doing the same library job. How many pairs can the teacher assign?
questions.hint: Compare a list made by choosing a first and second name with the actual pair.

questions.title: A balanced box
questions.prompt: A shelf has 5 different mystery books and 4 different science books. A box must hold 3 books, including at least one from each group. How many different boxes can be packed?
questions.hint: The box can contain either one or two mystery books.

questions.title: The captain’s badge
questions.prompt: Five hikers include two trained navigators. A team of three needs at least one navigator. One of the selected navigators must wear the captain’s badge. How many different team-and-captain choices are possible?
questions.hint: Choose the person who wears the badge before choosing the other two.

lessons.headline: Recover a doubling pattern from its total
lessons.intro: You can work backwards from a total when the pieces double. Write the pattern as equal starting shares, then ask how many shares the whole collection contains. That lets you recover a first term or a missing part.

example.prompt: Three piles double in size from left to right and contain 42 buttons altogether. How many buttons are in the smallest pile?
steps: The piles contain 1, 2 and 4 copies of the smallest pile. In total that makes 7 equal shares.
Each share holds 42 ÷ 7 = 6 buttons. The piles 6, 12 and 24 do add to 42.

lessons.bridge: Watch how the film lines up the doubled sum with the original and cancels the middle terms. The same relationship will let you uncover amounts even when the starting value is hidden.
lessons.recap: Mark whether the given number is one term, several terms, or the budget. Express the needed stretch of terms in starting shares. For a stopping claim, check the next full term against the balance.
lessons.videoTitle: Doubling, geometric growth and finite sums

questions.title: A segment of the trail
questions.prompt: The first trail marker has 4 stripes. Every later marker has twice as many as the previous one. How many stripes are on markers 3, 4 and 5 altogether?
questions.hint: Work out which marker has 16 stripes before adding.

questions.title: Back to day one
questions.prompt: A courier delivers twice as many parcels each day as on the previous day. After four days she has delivered 105 parcels altogether. How many did she deliver on day one?
questions.hint: How many copies of the first delivery make up four days?

questions.title: A missing tray
questions.prompt: Six trays hold 5, 10, 20, 40, 80 and 160 tiles. One entire tray is removed. The remaining trays hold 235 tiles together. How many tiles were on the missing tray?
questions.hint: Find the total of all six using the next doubling term.

questions.title: The badge factory
questions.prompt: A machine stamps twice as many badges every hour as in the hour before. Production through the end of hour 5 totals 186 badges. How many more badges are stamped in hour 7 alone than in the first five hours together?
questions.hint: First express the five-hour total as a number of equal first-hour batches.

lessons.headline: Keep neighbours together
lessons.intro: When two objects must be neighbours in a row, draw a bracket around them and move them as a unit. Think about what can change inside the bracket once the unit has a position.

example.prompt: Three different shells, amber, blue and cream, sit in a row. Amber must be immediately to the left of blue. How many rows are possible?
steps: The ordered block amber–blue and the cream shell are two objects to arrange. Either object can come first.
This gives amber–blue–cream or cream–amber–blue. The wording fixes the order inside the block.

lessons.bridge: In the film’s final row of cards, an arrangement can satisfy two neighbour rules at once. Watch what happens to that shared group when the question allows exactly one.
lessons.recap: Check whether the words fix the order inside a block. For a forbidden pair, count all rows and take away rows with that pair. For two conditions, decide whether their overlap should count once or disappear.

questions.title: The new arrivals
questions.prompt: Three pupils are already in a queue in the order Jo, Uma, Dev. Two more pupils, Eve and Tai, join together. They must be neighbours. The original three stay in their original order. How many queues are possible?
questions.hint: How many gaps in and around the existing queue can hold the pair?

questions.title: Along the bench
questions.prompt: Five different musicians sit in a row. The flute and the drum players may not sit next to each other. How many seatings are possible?
questions.hint: Count the forbidden seatings and subtract them from all the seatings.

questions.title: The sandwich
questions.prompt: Six different beads are threaded in a straight line from a marked end. The yellow bead must have the red bead and the green bead as its two immediate neighbours. How many lines are possible?
questions.hint: Turn all three special beads into one block. Which bead must be in its middle?

questions.title: Who sits beside Bea?
questions.prompt: Five friends, including Ana, Bea and Cal, take five seats in a row. Bea must sit next to exactly one of Ana and Cal. How many seatings work?
questions.hint: Count Bea beside Ana and Bea beside Cal separately. When do both descriptions apply?

lessons.headline: Find the area that is easier to see
lessons.intro: An awkward outline may become simple if you draw the rectangle around it. The whole area can be split into non-overlapping parts. If two shaded pieces cover the same place, keep track of that shared area as well.

example.prompt: A 6 cm by 5 cm photograph has a 2 cm by 3 cm rectangle cut from one corner. What area remains?
steps: The whole photograph covers 6 × 5 = 30 cm². The missing corner covers 2 × 3 = 6 cm².
The remaining L-shaped piece covers 30 − 6 = 24 cm².

figure.alt: A 6 by 5 cm rectangle with a 2 by 3 cm corner removed at the top right. Dashed lines show the missing outer corner.

lessons.bridge: Look for the corner triangle in the film and then the patch shaded twice. Watch why subtracting the two shaded rectangles needs one correction.
lessons.recap: Draw an easy surrounding shape and label each area you remove. A shared edge has zero area. An overlapping patch has positive area and must count only once.

questions.title: The noticeboard
questions.prompt: A noticeboard measures 8 cm by 7 cm on a plan. Two separate cards, 2 cm by 4 cm and 3 cm by 5 cm, lie fully inside it and do not overlap. What area is uncovered in square centimetres?
questions.hint: Start with the whole plan area, then subtract the two card areas.

questions.title: A diagonal corner
questions.prompt: A right triangle is cut from a corner of a 9 cm by 7 cm sheet. Its perpendicular sides along the sheet edges measure 5 cm and 4 cm. What area remains in square centimetres?
questions.hint: How much of a 5 cm by 4 cm rectangle does the triangle occupy?

questions.title: Crossing paths
questions.prompt: A rectangular park is 14 m long and 9 m wide. A 2 m wide path runs its full length. A 3 m wide path crosses it at right angles and runs the full width of the park. How many square metres of park lie outside both paths?
questions.hint: The crossing is a 2 m by 3 m rectangle. What happens to it if both path areas are subtracted?

questions.title: A tilted window
questions.prompt: On a 12 cm by 8 cm rectangular sheet, mark one point on each side. On the top it is 3 cm from the left corner. On the right it is 2 cm from the top. On the bottom it is 3 cm from the right. On the left it is 2 cm from the bottom. Join consecutive marks to form a window. What is the window area in square centimetres?
questions.hint: Draw the four corner triangles. Their perpendicular sides lie along the edges of the sheet.

lessons.headline: Count what is missing
lessons.intro: If a problem asks for at least one success, it can be easier to count outcomes with none. When two or three rules can hold at once, keep track of their shared outcomes before you subtract.

example.prompt: A bag can carry any two-letter label made from A, B and C, with repeats allowed. How many labels contain at least one A?
steps: All labels together number 3 × 3 = 9. A label with no A uses only B and C, giving 2 × 2 = 4.
The other 9 − 4 = 5 labels contain at least one A. This includes AA.

lessons.bridge: In the film, a student may appear on two lists, and a number may appear on three. Track one shared item as each list or overlap is counted.
lessons.recap: Define the whole set and write the precise opposite condition. For overlapping lists, subtract pair overlaps once. With three lists, restore their triple overlap once before subtracting the union.

questions.title: The night display
questions.prompt: Each of three windows can independently show a star, a moon or a cloud. How many displays have at least one cloud?
questions.hint: Count displays with clear skies first.

questions.title: A shared shelf
questions.prompt: Two shelves hold lists of recommended titles. The first list has 18, the second has 14, and the library finds 26 different titles across the two lists. How many titles appear on both?
questions.hint: By how much does the sum of the separate lengths exceed the number of different titles?

questions.title: Skip the markers
questions.prompt: Banners are numbered from 10 through 50 inclusive. A banner is marked if its number is a multiple of 4 or 6. How many banners remain unmarked?
questions.hint: Count multiples inside the stated interval. Common multiples of 4 and 6 repeat every 12.

questions.title: Three stamps
questions.prompt: At an expo 40 visitors can choose which stamps to collect, including none. Twenty collect Shell, 18 collect Leaf and 16 collect Star. There are 9 with Shell and Leaf, 7 with Shell and Star, and 6 with Leaf and Star. Each pair count includes the 3 visitors with all three. How many visitors have no stamp?
questions.hint: Follow a visitor with three stamps through “add the single lists, subtract the pair lists”.

lessons.headline: How often did you count each object?
lessons.intro: A match has two players, and each player can report playing in it. If you add their reports, every match appears twice. Other problems use three people per group or different numbers in different groups. Choose one thing to count from both sides.

example.prompt: Four children each write a card to each of the other three. How many cards are written?
steps: Each child writes three separate cards. Counting by writers gives 4 × 3 = 12 cards.
Each card has one writer. A card travelling the opposite way is a different card, so all 12 count.

lessons.bridge: Compare those cards with the film’s handshakes. Then follow one helper-room booking as it is counted first by room and then by helper.
lessons.recap: Name the object before adding reports. A match has two endpoints; a booking links one person to one place. Divide only by the number of times your counting rule records each object.

questions.title: Glass triangles
questions.prompt: Six triangular glass pieces meet at one shared corner. All their other corners are separate. One dot marks each distinct corner position. How many dots are there?
questions.hint: Count the corners that belong to just one triangle, then the corner they all share.

questions.title: Inside a wheel
questions.prompt: A wheel drawing has 9 points evenly spaced on its rim and one at its centre. An edge joins every pair of consecutive rim points, including the last and first. There is also one spoke from each rim point to the centre. How many edges are drawn?
questions.hint: Count the edges touching each rim point and the centre, or count rim edges and spokes separately.

questions.title: Workshop rota
questions.prompt: At camp, 8 pupils each attend 2 workshops and 6 other pupils each attend 3. The drama workshop has 4 pupils. Every other workshop has 5. How many workshops are there altogether?
questions.hint: Count pupil–workshop bookings, then account for the drama bookings separately.

questions.title: Friends at the party
questions.prompt: Eight people are at a party. Friendship goes both ways. Everyone has either three or four friends among the others. Altogether there are 14 different pairs of friends. How many people have four friends?
questions.hint: Imagine first giving everyone three reported friendships. Compare that with the number of endpoints of 14 pairs.

lessons.headline: One or two short of a full group
lessons.intro: Take 11 counters. Groups of 3 leave 2 loose, and groups of 4 leave 3 loose. In each case the loose counters are just one short of a full group. Moving every candidate by the same small amount can turn two different remainders into one common-multiple problem.

example.prompt: What is the smallest positive number that leaves 3 when divided by 4 and 5 when divided by 6?
steps: Both remainders are one short of the group size. Add 1, and the new number must be divisible by both 4 and 6.
Their first positive common multiple is 12. Undo the shift to get 11, and check both remainders.

lessons.bridge: On the film’s ruler, watch the two endpoints move with the candidates. When the marks slide back, notice whether the last one still lies inside the original interval.
lessons.recap: Check how far each remainder is from a full group. If the same shift works for every divisor, shift both ends of the interval too. Undo the shift and include or exclude endpoints exactly as the question says.

questions.title: Two empty spaces
questions.prompt: A tin contains a positive number of buttons. Filling trays of 5 leaves 3 buttons loose. Filling trays of 7 leaves 5 loose. What is the smallest possible number of buttons?
questions.hint: Both partial trays need two more buttons.

questions.title: The missing digit
questions.prompt: A three-digit number begins with 73. It is divisible by both 4 and 3. What is its final digit?
questions.hint: Test the last two digits for divisibility by 4, then test the digit sum.

questions.title: Between the gates
questions.prompt: A number is greater than 46 and at most 118. It leaves 4 when divided by 6 and 6 when divided by 8. How many such numbers are there?
questions.hint: Add 2 to both ends. Is the lower gate included?

questions.title: The leftover marble
questions.prompt: A collector has between 100 and 200 marbles, including the endpoints. Packing them in trays of 7 leaves 1 marble. Packing them in trays of 9 also leaves 1 marble. The total is even. How many marbles are there?
questions.hint: What change would remove the identical leftover from either type of packing?

lessons.headline: Give every possibility one home
lessons.intro: An awkward count becomes shorter when you split it into groups. Choose a feature that every outcome has exactly once, such as the position of a special item. Then count each group using just the rules that apply to it.

example.prompt: There are two hats, one plain and one striped, and three scarves, one plain and two different striped ones. How many hat-and-scarf outfits have exactly one striped item?
steps: Striped hat with plain scarf makes one outfit. Plain hat with a striped scarf makes two.
The striped item is in a different place in the two groups. Add 1 + 2 to get 3 outfits.

lessons.bridge: In the film’s exhibit puzzle, use the colour of the middle room to read each case. Notice which case has an extra restriction on exhibit B.
lessons.recap: Name the feature that puts an outcome in a row. Check that every allowed outcome has exactly one row, then add the row counts. Read a restriction inside its own case before carrying it into another.

questions.title: Biscuit box
questions.prompt: Choose one biscuit from each of two trays. The first tray has two different iced biscuits and one plain biscuit. The second has one iced biscuit and four different plain biscuits. How many choices give exactly one iced biscuit?
questions.hint: Which tray can supply the iced biscuit?

questions.title: At the starting line
questions.prompt: Four different runners line up. Ava must be either first or last. In how many different orders can they stand?
questions.hint: Count Ava at each end as its own case.

questions.title: The short password
questions.prompt: A password is a row of three different symbols chosen from A, B, C, 1 and 2. It must start with a letter and include at least one digit. How many passwords are possible?
questions.hint: After the first letter, classify the last two places by how many digits they contain.

questions.title: The three stops
questions.prompt: A guide chooses three different stops in order from an arch, a bridge, a cave, a dock and an orchard. The arch must be included. When the arch is the middle stop, the orchard cannot be visited. How many itineraries are allowed?
questions.hint: Split according to the position of the arch. Apply the orchard rule only when it is in force.

lessons.headline: Follow the truth of the whole claim
lessons.intro: In these puzzles each person either always tells the truth or always lies. A proposed assignment works only when every statement has the right truth value for its speaker. Sometimes two claims fix a relationship before you can name a single truth-teller.

example.prompt: Bo always lies. He says, “Mira is a liar.” What must Mira be?
steps: Bo’s statement must be false. So the description “Mira is a liar” is false.
The only other possibility is that Mira is truthful.

lessons.bridge: When Kai says both people are liars in the film, test the whole sentence. Then follow the links in the four-person puzzle and notice which statement becomes settled first.
lessons.recap: Translate each speaker’s words into a condition. A truthful speaker must match it and a liar must contradict it. For “both” to be false, just one part needs to fail. Check every claim in the final assignment.

questions.title: The sealed envelope
questions.prompt: Exactly one of two envelopes, red and gold, has a ticket. Tess always lies. She says, “The gold envelope is empty.” Which envelope has the ticket? Enter red or gold.
questions.hint: The whole claim about the gold envelope must be false.

questions.title: The two switches
questions.prompt: Each of two switches is on or off. A liar says, “Both switches are on.” You can see that the left switch is on. Is the right switch on or off? Enter on or off.
questions.hint: With the left switch already on, what would make the whole sentence false?

questions.title: Is the gate open?
questions.prompt: Exactly one of Lee and Mo always tells the truth. The other always lies. Lee says, “Mo tells the truth and the gate is open.” Mo says, “The gate is closed.” Is the gate open or closed? Enter open or closed.
questions.hint: Test the two possible gate positions. Count how many speakers would be truthful in each case.

questions.title: The lighthouse crew
questions.prompt: Each crew member always tells the truth or always lies. Ari says, “Bev is a liar.” Bev says, “Cy is a liar.” Cy says, “Ari and Bev are the same type.” How many of the three are truthful?
questions.hint: Use Ari’s statement to determine a relationship between Ari and Bev before deciding either type.
